concepts.title: Data and Graphical Representation
concepts.definition: The information collected in all such cases (runs of a batsman, wickets of a bowler, marks of students) is called data. Data is usually collected in the context of a situation that we want to study. A Pictograph is a pictorial representation of data using symbols. A bar graph is a display of information using bars of uniform width, their heights being proportional to the respective values. A double bar graph is a bar graph showing two sets of data simultaneously; it is useful for the comparison of the data.
concepts.formula: bar height proportional to value; bars of equal width with equal gaps
concepts.key_idea: Data organised and shown with pictographs, bar graphs or double bar graphs.

concepts.title: Circle Graph or Pie Chart
concepts.definition: A circle graph shows the relationship between a whole and its parts. The whole circle is divided into sectors. The size of each sector is proportional to the activity or information it represents. The proportion of a sector = number of items in the sector / whole. A circle graph is also called a pie chart.
concepts.key_idea: Pie chart: each sector is a fraction of the whole circle.

concepts.title: Drawing Pie Charts (Central Angle)
concepts.definition: The total angle at the centre of a circle is 360 degrees. The central angle of the sectors will be a fraction of 360 degrees. To draw a pie chart: (1) draw a circle with any convenient radius and mark its centre O and a radius OA; (2) use the protractor to draw each sector angle; (3) continue marking the remaining sectors.
concepts.key_idea: Central angle of a sector = fraction of 360 degrees.

concepts.title: Reading Values from a Pie Chart
concepts.definition: A pie chart gives each sector as a percentage of the whole. To find an actual amount, use the unitary method: if a given percent represents a known amount, then 1 percent represents amount / percent, and the required percent represents (amount / percent) x target_percent.
concepts.formula: required amount = (given amount / given percent) x target percent
concepts.key_idea: Use the unitary method to convert between percentages and amounts.

concepts.title: Random Experiments and Equally Likely Outcomes
concepts.definition: Such an experiment where the result cannot be controlled (like tossing a coin giving Head or Tail) is called a random experiment; Head or Tail are the two outcomes of this experiment. Outcomes of an experiment are equally likely if each has the same chance of occurring. A random experiment is one whose outcome cannot be predicted exactly in advance.
concepts.formula: equally likely: each outcome has the same chance
concepts.key_idea: A random experiment has outcomes that cannot be predicted; equally likely means same chance.

concepts.title: Probability of an Event
concepts.definition: Each outcome of an experiment or a collection of outcomes makes an event. Probability of an event = number of outcomes that make an event / total number of outcomes of the experiment, when the outcomes are equally likely. For example, the probability of getting a head when a coin is tossed = 1/2; the probability of getting an even number on a die is 3/6. The probability of an event not happening = 1 - probability of the event (probability it rains 1/10, probability it does not rain 9/10).
concepts.key_idea: Probability = outcomes making the event divided by total outcomes.
